headline: Brent is trading near $91 as a 5.28 million barrel API crude build outweighs a new ADNOC vessel attack in Hormuz and US-Iran strikes across the Gulf, so today's EIA report and the Trump-Xi-Putin summit are the next tests.
overview: Brent January settled at $93.14 on Tuesday (+0.76%) and WTI at $86.01 (+0.34%), supported by tanker attacks in Hormuz and Iranian drone strikes on Bahrain. Prices fell in Asia after API data showed a 5.28 million barrel US crude build against an expected small draw. Reuters-based reports had Brent January near $92.5 and WTI near $84.8 early in the session. The supplied quotes at 08:47 UTC show January Brent at $91.33 and December WTI at $83.81, so the market kept falling even after an ADNOC vessel attack was reported. Note that the headline prices supplied (Brent $88.69, WTI $82.64) match the second-month contracts, so the quoted 24-hour falls of 4.0% and 3.5% partly reflect a contract mismatch. On the front months, Brent is about 1.9% and WTI about 2.6% below Tuesday's settlements (my calculation).

developments.title: ADNOC L&S vessel attacked in Strait of Hormuz; one crew member missing, 11 injured
developments.summary: ADNOC Logistics & Services said one of its vessels was attacked while transiting the Strait of Hormuz on the evening of 17 November. One crew member is missing and 11 are injured, and the remaining crew were evacuated. Search and rescue operations are under way. The company statement, carried by WAM, did not say who carried out the attack or what type of vessel was hit. Bloomberg, via a Rigzone-based summary, described an intraday Brent swing of about $3 on Tuesday on new ship attacks.
developments.why_it_matters: A single logistics vessel does not remove barrels, but a second consecutive session of attacks on UAE-linked shipping raises war-risk costs and the chance that operators hold back cargoes. The market has so far faded these headlines unless loadings or transits fall, so the effect is likely a floor under prices rather than a rally.

developments.title: US strikes IRGC missile site on Qeshm; Gulf states intercept Iranian and Houthi missiles and drones
developments.summary: A US military official said US jets hit an IRGC missile launch site on Qeshm Island on Tuesday, describing it as self-defence after Iranian drones were launched at a US facility in Bahrain. Iranian officials confirmed explosions on the island but said no critical infrastructure was damaged. On Wednesday, Bahrain and Kuwait said they had intercepted Iranian attacks, and Reuters reported that Gulf states had downed Iranian and Houthi missiles and drones. Bahrain said it had repelled Iranian air attacks three times this week. Diplomacy continues through Qatar and Oman.
developments.why_it_matters: The exchanges are on the Hormuz shoreline and against US bases, not against export terminals, so no barrels have been removed. The risk is a miscalculation that hits Gulf energy infrastructure, which would reprice the curve quickly. The Jan-Feb Brent spread of $2.64 shows the market still pays for prompt barrels. I found no new reporting on the two-day Hormuz reopening plan from the previous briefing.

developments.title: API reports a 5.28 million barrel US crude build and a large gasoline build
developments.summary: The API estimated that US crude inventories rose by 5.28 million barrels in the week to 13 November, against an expected draw of about 500,000 barrels per Trading Economics. Gasoline rose by 5.12 million barrels and distillates by 351,000 barrels. Cushing fell by 1.69 million barrels. The Brent-WTI gap widened to its largest in more than two weeks, and Sparta Commodities' June Goh said WTI arbitrage to Asia and northwest Europe remains shut.
developments.why_it_matters: Two consecutive large crude builds (9.0 million barrels the week before) and a big gasoline build point to weak export pull and soft refined-product demand. This weighs more on WTI than on Brent. The API figure is an industry estimate and often differs from the EIA print due at 15:30 UTC.

developments.title: Hormuz throughput recovering but still fragile
developments.summary: An article attributes to a US source (the name is truncated in the retrieved text) that Hormuz oil flows rose 78% in the third quarter to 9.1 million barrels per day, still well below a year earlier. ANZ said throughput is only about 49% of pre-war levels, with more exports forced onto alternative routes. LSEG vessel data suggest flows cannot yet normalise under current conditions. Reuters reported on Monday that six tankers caught fire in mine incidents on Sunday and Monday.
developments.why_it_matters: The surplus case rests on Gulf exports recovering, but flows at about half of pre-war levels leave the market exposed to any further attack. The attacks so far have slowed the recovery rather than reversed it, which explains why prices fall on data and bounce on incidents.

developments.title: Houthis hold Bab el-Mandeb coast; coalition reports intercepting a Houthi cruise missile aimed at Riyadh
developments.summary: Saudi-backed southern forces said on Sunday they had redeployed from Dhubab and the Bab el-Mandeb area to defend Aden, leaving the Houthis in control of the coastline. NBC reported that the Houthis have fired ballistic missiles at Saudi airports and oil facilities since the Yemen war restarted. Gulf News' live blog carried a headline that the coalition intercepted a Houthi cruise missile aimed at Riyadh. A WTOP headline says Saudi-backed forces launched a major attack on the Houthis, but I could not retrieve the article to verify it.
developments.why_it_matters: Houthi control of the strait's Yemeni shore adds tail risk to Saudi Red Sea exports from Yanbu, which have grown in importance while Hormuz is impaired. No tanker disruption at Bab el-Mandeb is reported yet, so the effect is on the risk premium only.

developments.title: Trump-Xi-Putin summit in Shenzhen on Thursday, with Iran and Hormuz on the agenda
developments.summary: China confirmed on Monday that Xi Jinping will meet Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump in Shenzhen on Thursday, the first meeting of the three leaders. The White House said it intends to prioritise nuclear non-proliferation and the Middle East war. Qatar is still trying to negotiate an interim deal to restore Hormuz traffic, and Trump has said renewed US strikes on Iran are highly unlikely if talks progress. An Indian market commentator quoted by Zee Business expects restraint around the summit, which is opinion.
developments.why_it_matters: A visible Chinese or Russian role in a Hormuz framework would cut the risk premium and add to the surplus narrative. A failed summit, or an escalation during it, would do the opposite. Today's Gulf strikes show the diplomatic and military tracks are running in parallel.

developments.title: US equities weak: S&P 500 at lowest close since July
developments.summary: CNBC's 17 November market report headline cited a Dow fall of more than 800 points and the lowest S&P 500 close since July. Treasury yields were little changed. The Fed's October minutes (meeting of 27-28 October) are due at 14:00 ET today.
developments.why_it_matters: Risk-off equity trading adds to demand-side caution for oil. A hawkish reading of the minutes would support the dollar and add pressure. The report did not state the cause of the equity fall, so the link to oil is indirect.

developments.title: Ukrainian drones reportedly hit Afipsky and Ilsky refineries in Krasnodar
developments.summary: Drones attacked the Afipsky and Ilsky refineries in Krasnodar Krai overnight on 18 November. The regional operational headquarters said fires broke out at two enterprises from falling drone debris and four people were injured. Ukrainian monitoring channels reported both refineries hit. No verified evidence of damage to processing units has been published. Their combined nameplate capacity is about 12.9 million tonnes a year, roughly 260,000 barrels per day (my conversion).
developments.why_it_matters: Refinery outages cut Russian product output and exports, which supports diesel and gasoline cracks. They slightly raise Russian crude available for export, so the net effect on crude is small. Outage duration is unknown until damage is confirmed.

verdict.reasoning: The strongest bearish argument is inventory and balance evidence: a second large API crude build, a 5.12 million barrel gasoline build, a shut WTI export arbitrage, Goldman's surplus call and a market that has already fallen about 18% in 30 days. The dashboard rules also show sell signals on intraday and lean sell for WTI swing. The strongest bullish argument is the escalation: an ADNOC vessel attack with a missing crew member, US strikes on Qeshm, Iranian and Houthi launches at Gulf states, Houthi control of the Bab el-Mandeb coast and Hormuz throughput at only about half of pre-war levels. Light positioning (11.6th percentile) and a steep Jan-Feb Brent backwardation of $2.64 mean a shock can reverse prices quickly. For the next 24 hours I give the edge to the bearish side, because the market has repeatedly sold on stock data despite similar incidents, but only modestly. Today's EIA print and the Shenzhen summit could move that balance either way, and a hit on Gulf export infrastructure would override it. Today's quoted price falls are also exaggerated by a contract mismatch in the supplied data.
